title: Why a held-out set estimates generalisation
promptMarkdown:
In under 200 words and without the lesson open:

1. State the assumption under which the error on a held-out set is an unbiased estimate of the risk of a trained model, and show in one line why the training error is not.
2. Explain why choosing the best of several models by their *test* error destroys the property in (1), and what the validation set is for.
3. Give one concrete example of leakage that would survive a perfectly executed random train/test split.
hintLadder: Conditional on the fitted model, what is the distribution of the loss on one held-out item? What does that give for the expectation of the average?
The minimum of several noisy unbiased estimates is not unbiased. In which direction is it biased?
Random splitting removes selection by the experimenter, not structure in the data: think of time, groups or duplicated items.

criteria.criterion: States that the held-out data must be independent of the training data and of every decision used to fit the model; conditional on the model the held-out losses are i.i.d. with mean equal to the risk, whereas the trained model was chosen to minimise the training error.

levels.label: met
levels.description: Assumption stated and the one-line argument given.

levels.label: not met
levels.description: Missing or confuses with sample size.

criteria.criterion: Explains that selecting on the test error makes the chosen model's test error the minimum of noisy estimates and therefore optimistic; the validation set absorbs this role so the test set can be used once.

levels.label: met
levels.description: Both the bias direction and the role of the validation set.

criteria.criterion: Gives a correct example that random splitting does not prevent: temporal order, grouped records (same patient or machine), duplicates, target-derived features, or preprocessing fitted on all data.

levels.label: met
levels.description: Correct example with the route of the leak.
